Bhante, in 'web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02' (web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02), what is the core doctrinal teaching regarding 'One thing only] Luang Pu once'?

In this section from *web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02*, the master explains: *"One thing only] Luang Pu once said, “In the Rains Retreat of 1952 I made a vow to read the entire Canon to see where the endpoint of the Buddha’s teachings lay—to see where the end of the noble truths, the end of suffering, lay—to see how the Buddha had summarized it."*. From the perspective of the Four Noble Truths, suffering arises whenever the mind grasps at impermanent phenomena (*anicca*) as a reliable self (*atta*). By establishing clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) and seeing conditioned events as empty of inherent ownership, craving (*taṇhā*) is unhooked. It is like grasping a poisonous cobra by the tail: tempting and sleek from afar, but deadly the moment you grasp it. Release the tail and live in safety. Anchor your understanding in direct seeing rather than speculative theory.

In sitting meditation, how do we work with the body and breath when 'web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02' advises: 'I read the Canon to the'?

The practical guidance given in *web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02* instructs: *"I read the Canon to the end, contemplating along the way, but there was no passage that made contact deeply enough in the mind that I could say for sure, ‘This is the end of suffering."*. When you sit on the cushion, do not wage war against wandering thoughts. First ground attention in the physical posture—soften the belly, relax the face, and allow the breath to find its natural rhythm. When thoughts arise, notice the space around them rather than following the story. It is like still, flowing water (nam lai rin): awareness flows smoothly perceiving sights and sounds, while the heart inside remains utterly motionless. Rest the mind gently in the rhythm of each natural in-and-out breath.

What advice is given in 'web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02' (web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02) for overcoming habitual reactivity regarding: 'Sāriputta had just come out of'?

Addressing everyday distress, the text emphasizes: *"Sāriputta had just come out of the attainment of the cessation, and the Buddha asked him, ‘Sāriputta, your skin is especially bright, your complexion especially clear."*. When emotional turbulence or conflict flares, the ego habitually wants to blame external circumstances. The Forest masters remind us that outer events are merely triggers; the actual suffering is the inner contraction of resistance. Step back for a single conscious breath, recognize the tightness as impermanent, and respond with patient goodwill. It is like an old brass spittoon: people may spit into it or polish it, but it never gets angry or vain. It simply does its duty without ego. Meet daily challenges with a spacious, generous heart.

In 'web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02' (web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02), how does the simile of the deep anchor in a mountain lake illuminate the teaching: 'What is the dwelling place of'?

In this section of *web books giftsheleftbehind section0032 html 746c02*, the Dhamma is brought to life: *"What is the dwelling place of your mind?’ “Ven."*. The Forest Tradition relies on direct nature imagery because the mind operates through experiential resonance rather than abstract logic. It is like a small boat moored to a deep anchor on a vast mountain lake: waves may roll on the surface, but the anchor keeps the boat steady. When you hold this simile in your heart during practice, it provides an immediate reference point for letting go and realizing unburdened clarity.
